title: AWS Lambda Now Runs GPU Inference with 48 Concurrent Invocations Sharing One Model per GPU
summary:
AWS Lambda now runs Event Functions on EC2 G-series GPU instances through Lambda Managed Instances, with up to 48 concurrent invocations sharing one model per GPU, vLLM and SGLang base images that need no handler code, and 90-minute asynchronous timeouts. Billing is the instance price plus a 9.75 percent fee; first hands-on tests report an eight-minute publish and no response streaming.

By Steef-Jan Wiggers

title: Context as a Resource
summary: Managing concurrent tasks across separate agent sessions quickly exhausts human attention, motivating always-on personal agents behind a single continuous interface. Yet when every context shares identical frozen backbone weights, funneling interleaved dialogues and external events into one linear session induces cross-topic constraint bleed and head-of-line stalling. Conversely, router-ticket hierarchies incur lossy prose handoffs, heavy routing overhead, and blind merges - collapsing true-conflict repository merges to a 33.3% three-run mean despite high isolated branch passes. Rather than scheduling anthropomorphic roles, we introduce ClonAct, a routerless architecture that virtualizes context blocks directly through a pluggable single-pass non-generative Context MMU, in-place Context Cells, a footprint-aware Synaptic Bus with an isolated trial merge gate, and a wave-flushed Shared Trunk. Across three programmatic multi-stream benchmarks and three model families, our portable trial merge gate lifts true-conflict merges to 63.3%, while ClonAct's routerless virtualization attains this ceiling with 45.9% fewer prompt tokens and prevents compact-model router collapse. Under continuous surge streams, ClonAct matches top completion (95.0%) with the lowest median wait and zero timed-out status checks.

title: Using a "chaos loop" to harden the Claude Docs launch: 60 server errors across billions of requests
summary: Claude Docs is a doc editor that you, your teammates, and Claude all work in together. The interesting part is that a Claude session anywhere, from chat to Claude Code, can open the same doc and read, write, and comment in it live, right next to you. story_key: model:claude|title:using a chaos loop to harden the claude docs launch 60 server errors across bill
content_excerpt: Claude Docs is a doc editor that you, your teammates, and Claude all work in together. The interesting part is that a Claude session anywhere, from chat to Claude Code, can open the same doc and read, write, and comment in it live, right next to you. We released Docs on September 16, 2026. This post is about the service that runs underneath it. Three weeks before Claude Docs opened to the public, it was running as a proof of concept on a single node, used by a few thousand people inside Anthropic. We were racing toward an ambitious launch date, and our own estimate said we'd see millions of docs within the first few days. We launched on September 16. By September 22, people had created over 4.6 million docs. Across 2 billion requests we saw only 60 server errors, and we never had to roll back. The whole Docs service ran on about 50 memory-optimized pods. But honestly, this only worked because our frontier models have gotten much better recently (I used an internal research model roughly comparable to Claude Fable 5.2). In our experience, they can now stick with one goal through a run like this for weeks, which is what helped us hit launch scale in a tight timeline. A few thousand internal users on one machine told us nothing about whether the service would survive launch, and we obviously didn't have launch traffic to test with. We wanted real evidence to decide how fast we could roll out. So on September 4, about two weeks before launch, I had Claude drive a staging cluster that mirrored production at over a million synthetic docs a day and break core components on purpose. And then... I just left it running (I've included the full cost at the end of this article). My setup was pretty simple. The loop was a session in Claude Code that I left running: pick a scenario, run the harness, read the telemetry, propose a fix, ship it to staging, repeat. That session acted as a coordinator and handed most of the work to sub-agents. In the busiest week, that usually meant about 11 sub-agents running at a time, and 30 at the peak. The coordinator also talked to our internal variant of Claude Tag (beta) via the Slack MCP to learn from other infrastructure teams at Anthropic who had scaled similar services. Their agents checked our scaling approach for pitfalls they’d already hit. Each iteration looked the same. title: HabitusMem: Belief Memory over Evolving User Preferences for LLM Agents
summary: Personalized LLM agents must act on a user's current preferences, which change across interactions and are rarely stated in full. Existing memory systems store and retrieve content from the interaction history and leave the agent to work out which preferences still hold and where they apply. Such content does not indicate whether a preference is still current or where it applies, so agents often act on outdated or misapplied preferences. We instead treat memory as the assistant's belief about the user. Following Bourdieu's account of habitus as durable but revisable dispositions, we model the user as a latent preference state that every interaction, including the current request, both reveals and updates. The belief summarizes what the history supports about this state, and memory consists of the individual beliefs that bear on the agent's current decision, each with its evidence, scope, and status. We implement this view in HabitusMem, a trained writer that states these beliefs as text records for a frozen agent. Across two agent families, HabitusMem achieves the best results among memory systems on both PersonaMem-v2 and VitaBench 2.0. Controlled analyses show that learned request conditioning drives the answering gain, while auxiliary training tasks improve tool use.

title: How Public Evals Work and Fail, and What Should Change
summary: How to read eval scores and what to question, from a teardown of 12 benchmarks.
story_key: story|title:how public evals work and fail and what should change
content_excerpt: As models ship faster, eval scores are often the first thing we learn about a new model. But how much weight should we put in them? In eight of twelve public evals studied, there’s evidence the grader failed work that should have passed. And even when the grader gets it right, many benchmarks measure what’s easy rather than what matters, and should instead focus on reliability, work velocity, multi-turn collaboration, etc. Here, we’ll cover the common patterns and principles, the errors models make, and where current benchmarks fall short. I’ll also share what we’re getting wrong and what should change, including why average pass rate isn’t enough and why dollars are the wrong measure of cost. Finally, we’ll walk through twelve evals: four on coding and science, six on knowledge work, and two on browsing and computer use. By the end, you’ll know what to trust in a benchmark and what to question. In addition, eval benchmarks are increasingly maintained like software. They ship versioned releases and accept fixes through issues and pull requests. Agents’ Last Exam v1.1 retired 30 tasks and revised 57 others, and Harvey LAB’s public set has grown from about 1,250 tasks to 2,010 since launching in May 2026. Like software, these releases can also introduce breaking changes—Terminal Bench can drop saturated tasks with each version, making scores hard to compare across releases. Deterministic checks over LLM judges. Code-based checks are reproducible and won’t shift rankings when a judge model is updated. DeepSWE and AutomationBench avoid LLM judges altogether, and Agents’ Last Exam goes to great lengths to minimize them. When an eval does need a judge—for a legal memo or clinical response—it narrows the judge’s job to binary yes/no rubric items rather than a holistic score. Graders check the outcome, not the steps. The intent is to allow any approach that produces the right result to pass. For example, Terminal Bench inspects the final state of the container and ignores the agent’s intermediate commands or console output. AutomationBench, OSWorld 2.0, and DeepSWE work the same way. All-pass scoring is common because partial work often isn’t usable. Under all-pass scoring, a task passes only if every test or criterion passes. DeepSWE, Terminal Bench, Terminal Bench Science, AutomationBench, and Harvey LAB score this way. As Harvey puts it, “there is no partial credit for catching most of the issues”—a report that flags eight of ten risks is incomplete, not 80% us

title: COVERAGE-TRACE: Source-Side Counterfactual Tracing for Detecting Omissions in LLM Summaries
summary:
Omissions are difficult to verify because missing information leaves no output span
to inspect: a summary may be factually supported while still excluding a decision, qualification, quantity, or condition needed to preserve the source's meaning. We introduce COVERAGE-TRACE, a source-side counterfactual framework that evaluates omission as dependence on a designated atomic source fact. It replaces only the target fact with type-matched alternatives, holds the candidate summary fixed, and measures the resulting change in its teacher-forced, length-normalized likelihood. A summary covering the target should respond more strongly than one omitting it, while aggregation across multiple counterfactuals reduces sensitivity to replacement choice.
  We evaluate COVERAGE-TRACE on 80 matched covered--omitted QMSum pairs spanning several fact types and four open-weight models. Multi-CF achieves 0.764--0.825 AUROC, compared with 0.640 for the strongest evaluated text-only baseline. On Falcon-7B, targeted interventions achieve 0.779 AUROC, whereas shuffling counterfactual assignments reduces performance to 0.533; target deletion is effective while unrelated deletion is not. However, adjustment for meaning-preserving paraphrases reduces AUROC to 0.591--0.624.
  COVERAGE-TRACE therefore provides a practical, complementary signal of target-specific source--summary dependence, but not a wording-invariant semantic coverage probability. These results establish source-side intervention as a promising approach to omission detection while identifying semantic invariance as the central remaining challenge.

title: How Abundant designed efficient rollout architecture with Modal Sandboxes
summary: Abundant builds RL environments that run on Modal Sandboxes, powering training for frontier labs.
story_key: model:modal|title:how abundant designed efficient rollout architecture with modal sandboxes
content_excerpt: Abundant builds reinforcement learning environments that frontier labs like OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Meta use to train and evaluate their models. Labs improve agent capability by giving them difficult tasks that Abundant designs, letting the model attempt it, and grading the result as pass or fail. Each task is an RL rollout with a full environment. The model needs instructions, a defined goal, and a verifier to decide whether the task was completed. But it also needs infrastructure: compute to power the run, Dockerfiles, and isolation. Depending on the task, an agent may even need accelerators like GPUs. Abundant has created over 75,000 rollouts — ranging from GPU kernel optimization to long-horizon coding — each of which runs in a Modal Sandbox. Modal makes their rollout infrastructure easy to build and cost-efficient to run, enabling the Abundant team to focus on their core business. Today, almost all of Abundant’s rollout platform runs on Modal. Modal Functions power Abundant’s scheduler API to start tasks, clean up dead runs, and review rollouts. Modal Sandboxes power the rollout environments. Abundant initially chose to evaluate Sandbox providers because they wanted to avoid managing EC2 clusters directly, which would pull engineering time away from their core business of building RL environments. Modal enabled them to build their infrastructure directly in code, launch Sandboxes easily via API, and elastically scale their traffic as business grew. As of November 2026, Abundant runs over two million Sandboxes per month. Modal worked with the Abundant team to design and build their rollout architecture, focusing on designing a system that didn’t leave Abundant having to pay heavily for idle compute. Each rollout has a few steps: launch the task, attempt the task, verify the work, and report the work. Throughout the rollout, a “monitor” needs to verify that the Sandbox is still active. While Abundant had considered hosting the monitor outside of the Sandbox, they ultimately chose to include the rollout monitor inside the Sandbox and then used short-lived Modal Functions to start Sandboxes. The small rollout monitor inside the Sandbox makes periodic HTTP calls: a heartbeat every 30 seconds, live events, and the final result. If a Sandbox goes quiet, the control plane will attempt to connect three times before terminating it. Abundant also needed to solve for Sandboxes that didn’t consume CPU and memory resources at consistent rates. The Modal team

  • Fixed ~/.claude.json sometimes being reset to defaults when a network stall or file lock made it unreadable and cleared during a save
  • Fixed repeated sign-outs on macOS when Claude Code could read the Keychain but not save to it. That session now stops at expiry and says why, and other sessions stay signed in

  • Fixed picking a cloud session in /teleport replacing your open conversation: the pick now starts a new session, as /clear does, and /resume brings the old one back

  • Fixed /code-review <pr number> sometimes reviewing the checked-out branch instead of the pull request without saying so: it now reads the pull request with gh pr diff, or says when it can't

  • Fixed Code Mode hiding a script's finished edits and the stopped command after Esc, and losing them on exit
  • Fixed a runaway loop in Code Mode filling the machine's memory; it is now stopped at a limit
  • Fixed a background agent running on when it was stopped while it was being resumed

  • Changed auto mode to run git status less often so most requests wait less in large repositories; a git command that discards changes may be blocked until the working tree is checked
  • Changed /code-review <pr number> --fix, and /code-review given a pull request URL, to stop without reviewing when gh pr diff is refused or fails
  • Changed 'Exit and stop tasks' to end this session's scheduled tasks so they don't run again on resume, unless you exit while Claude is responding
  • Changed some teammate panes to start through /bin/sh, so they may not read shell start-up files
  • Changed computer use on macOS to give up on an app launch that has not finished after 30 seconds
  • Gateway: Changed the start-up warning shown while access_control.allow_cidrs is empty to a notice at every start, boxed in text logs: never expose the gateway to the public internet
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed a second host name's clone of the same owner/name to go under _repos/clones/<host>/ in the base folder; no clone moves
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed repositories with unusual characters in their address path to clone anew in a new folder; rules and volumes naming the old one stop applying, and the old clone stays put
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed --repository-folder to take most folders in the base folder at --capacity 1 (above 1, one there stops start-up); another repository's session overlapping one is refused
  • Changed Code Mode so a PreToolUse hook that errors no longer refuses a script's tool call, as outside Code Mode; set "onFailure": "block" on a command, HTTP or MCP tool hook that must refuse
  • Changed Code Mode to refuse a script's read of a line range over 256 MiB, which could use gigabytes of memory, and fixed reads of very long lines timing out
  • Changed Code Mode to also start when telemetry, nonessential traffic or feature flags are turned off; an administrator can keep it off in managed settings
  • Changed Code Mode to run a script that declares its own log, preview or sleep, which it used to refuse
  • Changed macOS login renewal to test the Keychain with a Claude Code-write-check item
  • Changed the /tasks header and the footer's background count to one number covering shells, monitors, MCP calls, agents, workflows and scheduled tasks
  • Changed Stop and SubagentStop hooks to list a Monitor's script as monitor, not shell, in background_tasks
  • Removed 2.1.326's automatic retry at the limit named in a max_tokens error; behind a gateway whose model takes fewer output tokens, set CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS to that limit
  • [VSCode] Added a line above the message box after you decline the trust prompt, with Review trust to bring the prompt back without reloading the window
  • [VSCode] Fixed being signed out of Claude Code in every window and terminal when the sign-in server took 10 to 30 seconds to answer the extension's token refresh
  • [VSCode] Fixed keys pressed while an input method (IME) is composing moving focus on or declining a permission prompt, running menu rows and closing dialogs (#106358)
  • [VSCode] Fixed the permission prompt for Bash, Edit, Write and other built-in tools not showing why a safety check asks
  • [VSCode] Fixed a half-written plan comment being lost or moved to another passage, and an input method's Enter sending the comment, ending a session rename or picking an @-mentioned file
  • [VSCode] Fixed the limit banner not saying when usage credits are in use, and the session survey covering that banner and the usage credits card
  • [VSCode] Fixed screen readers not announcing a permission request that arrived while the Account & Usage dialog was open until that dialog was closed
  • [VSCode] Fixed a proposed-edit diff tab staying open, with an Accept button that did nothing, after its terminal Claude Code session disconnected
  • [VSCode] Fixed short tool inputs and outputs cut off at the panel's edge with no way to read the rest (they now open in an editor tab), and dragging to select text also opening one
  • [VSCode] Fixed the Up key putting an earlier message over text that an input method (IME) is composing in the message box (#101294)
  • [VSCode] Fixed dropping an Explorer folder onto the chat inserting nothing on VS Code 1.103 to 1.139 or in a floating chat window, and the drop highlight vanishing with a false "Hold Shift" hint
  • [VSCode] Fixed a permission prompt moving keyboard focus away from the details you were scrolling as its buttons switched on
  • [VSCode] Fixed file links in a Claude tab opening in another editor group when claudeCode.lockEditorGroups is off (#108884)
  • [VSCode] Fixed ranges written with a single tilde (3~5 … 7~10) losing their tildes and showing struck-through text between them; only ~~text~~ is struck through now
  • [VSCode] Fixed dictation errors wrapping into a narrow column, the spinner turning while a question card waits, and a NUL symbol after each letter in the output of a failed UTF-16 command
  • [VSCode] Changed Down to stop at the last item of a permission prompt instead of wrapping to Yes
  • [VSCode] Changed command output to show hidden characters and control sequences other than plain colors as symbols, so Persian, Khmer, Lao, Sinhala and Malayalam text can look broken or out of order

title: An updated Clairic and Clairic-flash are now open-weight, from the new Workers AI Superintelligence team
summary: Clairic graduates from preview, while Clairic-flash joins the repertoire on Workers AI. We’re doing an open-weight release for both extraction models.
story_key: story|variant:flash|title:an updated clairic and clairic flash are now open weight from the new workers ai
content_excerpt: Cloudflare has become a neolab. We’re building our own frontier AI models for our customers and the open-source community. Both extraction models are hosted on Workers AI and full open weights are available on Hugging Face . We’re also excited to re-introduce ourselves as the Workers AI superintelligence team, the frontier AI research team behind Clef , Clairic, and lots more in the works. This team is working quickly to push the AI frontier and build useful models for Cloudflare’s customers and the open source community. Since announcing Clairic in preview, we have received a ton of use cases and helpful feedback on how customers wanted to use an extraction model. We heard about use cases ranging from extracting data from images like receipts to reading values from support tickets. We knew that we wanted extraction to be the clear focus for the model, so it had to excel at reading from unstructured data. We decided to go back to the drawing board with Clairic and redesigned our architecture, differentiating this new version of Clairic from our preview release. For ordinary text and number extraction fields, we now use parallel slot autoregressive generation instead of a single forward pass. Each field uses the tokens it has already written to choose its next token, then stops at its own end marker. All the fields advance together in the serving batch, still giving lightning-fast latency per request. This boosted our accuracy in extraction for both text and images, and the trade-off in accuracy offsets the small latency cost. For computation, estimation, and extraction use cases, we trained special heads that can handle estimates, forecasts, durations, calculated dates, and explicit arithmetic. Although the model architecture evolved, we kept the parts of the typed API interface that make the answers useful: confidence scores, character spans, and probabilities are still intact with every request. The model is still incredibly fast and cheap. From the evals below, you can see how our newer versions of Clairic have greatly improved on extraction across text, images, PDFs, and more. There are no public extraction benchmarks yet, but we ran our internal evals for other emerging extraction models on the market, such as Liquid AI’s D1.2 (pipelined with Apple Vision for optical character recognition) and Scaledown’s Extract . Our Clairic models excel across extraction use cases, but take these evals as directional guidance since they are self-reported. We wanted

It picks the best cluster, fails over automatically, and authenticates every request with SigV4 and IAM over AWS PrivateLink.
